say.text: A 60-year-old man has a deep scald across the front of his neck and chest from a boiling urn. His voice is normal, he is calm, and he is speaking in full sentences.
What is your first move?

choices.label: Check the airway now and plan early intubation
Work out the Parkland volume and start the drip
Watch the neck and intubate only if he struggles
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which threat can close the airway within hours, and which task can wait a few minutes of charting.
Right. A deep neck burn is a named reason to intubate early, while the airway is still easy to secure, before oedema builds.
The airway is part of the primary survey, so it comes before any burn arithmetic.
That choice is not right.
Burn arithmetic belongs to the secondary survey. The airway belongs to the primary survey and can close within hours, so it cannot wait for the sums.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the order: the primary survey comes before any burn sum.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Waiting for stridor is tempting, because the patient looks fine now. But oedema builds over the first hours, so the window can shut before the signs appear.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: the plan is to secure the airway before oedema develops, not after stridor starts.

say.text: You are grading a burn on a patient's back before you count it toward the total.
Which description is a full-thickness burn?

choices.label: Dry white or leathery patch, painless to a pin, not blanching
Mottled patch, less painful than the skin, with slow refill
Wet pink blistered patch that is very painful to touch
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pain is the first clue most people reach for, but it is only one clue. What does the skin look like, and how does it refill?
Right. Full thickness is dry, white or leathery, insensate, and does not blanch.
That is why it needs excision and grafting later, so the depth call matters for the plan.
That choice is not right.
Less pain feels like deeper injury, but pain falls only partly with depth. A mottled burn with slow refill is deep partial, not full thickness.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at refill and colour before pain: slow refill points to a deep partial burn.

say.text: That is not quite right.
A wet, blistered, very painful patch is superficial partial thickness. It blanches and heals in about 2 to 3 weeks.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the blister base: a wet pink base is a superficial, not a full-thickness, picture.

say.text: A 45-year-old man has burns over the whole front of his trunk and both arms, with nothing on the legs or back.
Using the adult rule of nines, what total body surface area is burnt?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work out the front of the trunk on its own first. Then ask what each arm carries on the adult chart.
Right. The front of the trunk is 18%, and each arm is 9%, which gives 36%.
The adult chart is built from these blocks, and the total feeds the Parkland sum later.
That choice is not right.
Giving each arm the leg value is the swap. An arm is 9%, and a leg is 18%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so relearn the blocks: 9 for the head and each arm, 18 for each leg and each side of the trunk.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The front of the trunk is an 18% block. The head's 9% has been put on the trunk.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check each block against its place: the front of the trunk is not the head.

say.text: A cyclist is pulled from a garage fire. His pulse oximeter reads 100%, and a junior has written 'carbon monoxide excluded' in the notes.
What is the right correction?

choices.label: Nothing to correct: 100% means the blood carries enough oxygen
Not excluded: measure carboxyhaemoglobin rather than trust saturation
Accept the note, and recheck the oximeter in an hour
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A clean number on a monitor feels like a verdict. Ask what that number can and cannot tell apart.
Right. A pulse oximeter cannot separate carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading proves nothing.
Carboxyhaemoglobin on co-oximetry measures the poison itself, so that is the number to trust.
That choice is not right.
A saturation of 100% comes from light that cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so the reading gives no reassurance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: a normal saturation says nothing about carbon monoxide.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Repeating the same reading adds nothing. However often the oximeter is checked, it cannot see carboxyhaemoglobin.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: repeated readings from this probe carry the same blind spot.

say.text: A 40-year-old woman has a deep burn over the cartilage of her ear. The team wants a topical agent that gets into dead eschar.
Which agent fits, and what must you watch for?

choices.label: Mafenide, and watch for metabolic acidosis
Silver sulfadiazine, and watch for leucopenia
Silver nitrate, and watch for hyponatraemia
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Two things sit in one stem: which agent gets through the eschar, and what it does to the blood. Take them one at a time.
Right. Mafenide penetrates eschar, which suits cartilage, and it can cause metabolic acidosis.
It is painful on application, so plan analgesia with it.
That choice is not right.
Silver sulfadiazine is broad and painless, but it does not get into eschar, and eschar is the property this ear needs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: an agent's property and its side effect are different facts.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Silver nitrate stains black and can cause hyponatraemia, but it stays on the surface and does not penetrate eschar.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: pick the agent for what it does to the eschar, then check its side effect.

say.text: No hints from here on. Five cold questions, and Try again still works.
A 60 kg adult has a 30% scald, burned 2 hours ago, with no fluid given yet. Using 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, what hourly rate covers the rest of the first half?
Right. The whole formula is 7,200 mL, so the first half is 3,600 mL, timed from the burn.
Two hours have gone, so 3,600 mL over the remaining six hours is 600 mL/h.
⚠ Exam note: PYQ keys still use 4 mL/kg/%TBSA, while current practice starts lower and titrates. Do the sum as asked, then check the question's wording.
That choice is not right.
That runs the whole 24-hour total into the first window. Only the half belongs there, over 8 hours from the burn.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check which total goes into the 8-hour window.

say.text: That choice is not right.
That spreads the half over the full day. The first half is timed to the 8-hour window, not to 24 hours.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the clock: the first half is a short window, not a day.

say.text: That is not quite right.
That spreads the first half over all 8 hours. The clock started at the burn, so count the time already gone.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count from the burn, not from the moment you are working.

say.text: A 28-year-old is seen 2 hours after a cellar fire, with soot on his lips and a hoarse voice.
Which order of tests makes most sense?

choices.label: Co-oximetry now, bronchoscopy for the airway, film as baseline
Chest X-ray first; bronchoscopy only if the film is abnormal
Arterial blood gas alone, since it answers every question

say.text: Right. Co-oximetry measures carboxyhaemoglobin, and bronchoscopy looks at the airway directly.
A chest film is often normal early, so it serves as a baseline rather than the gate.
That choice is not right.
A chest film is often normal early, so a clear film does not clear the airway, and it cannot gate the bronchoscopy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at what an early film can and cannot show.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A blood gas reports gas exchange and, with co-oximetry, carboxyhaemoglobin. It cannot see soot or oedema in the airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the airway is seen with a bronchoscope, not read from a gas.

say.text: A 60 kg adult is on the formula rate. At hour 4, urine is 110 mL/h, and blood pressure is steady.
What do you do with the rate?

choices.label: Keep the formula rate; the calculated number is the plan
Raise the rate by a fifth to match the output
Reduce the rate and recheck urine output hourly

say.text: Right. Output this high means fluid is ahead of need, so the rate comes down and hourly urine guides the next step.
The formula sets the start, and urine output steers from there.
That choice is not right.
The formula gives a starting rate. A fixed rate ignores the urine, which is the signal that should change it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: the formula sets the start, and urine sets the rest.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Raising the rate when output is already high pushes more fluid into a patient who is passing plenty. Over-resuscitation causes oedema and compartment syndromes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction: high output asks for less fluid, not more.

say.text: A 15 kg child with a burn is 2 hours in. Urine has been 9 mL/h.
Is that enough?

choices.label: No: under target, so raise fluid toward about 15 mL/h
No: far below the 30 to 50 mL/h adult range
Yes: above the adult 0.5 mL/kg/h target

say.text: Right. A child's target is 1 mL/kg/h, so 15 kg gives about 15 mL/h, and 9 mL/h is under it.
Raise the fluid, then recheck the output hourly, as in an adult.
That choice is not right.
The conclusion points the right way, but the yardstick is wrong. 30 to 50 mL/h is an adult figure, and a child's target scales with weight.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the yardstick: a child's target is set per kilogram.

say.text: That choice is not right.
0.5 mL/kg/h is the adult target, half the child's figure. Using it makes 9 mL/h look adequate when it is low.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the adult figure per kilogram is half the child's.

say.text: Last question, cold. A patient with burns has just arrived.
Which step has to come before any burn numbers are worked out?

choices.label: Primary survey: airway, breathing and circulation first
Estimating the TBSA on the rule of nines chart
Writing the Parkland sum on the fluid chart

say.text: Right. Airway, breathing and circulation come first in the primary survey.
TBSA and the fluid sum are secondary-survey work, so they come after the airway is secured.
That choice is not right.
Estimating TBSA matters, but it is secondary-survey work. It cannot be the first step.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the order: the burn chart comes after the primary survey.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The Parkland sum is burn arithmetic. It comes after the primary survey, while the airway can still close.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the order: breathing and circulation are the first checks.

say.text: Airway first, then size the burn honestly, start with the formula, and let urine output steer the fluid.

cards.q: In a burn with a deep neck scald, what comes first?
cards.a: Check the airway now and plan early intubation, before oedema builds.

cards.q: Which test confirms inhalation injury, and why is a normal chest film not enough?
cards.a: Fibreoptic bronchoscopy shows the airway directly; an early chest film is often normal.
Dry, white or leathery, painless to a pin, does not blanch. Pain alone does not grade depth.

cards.q: Adult rule of nines: what does the head carry, and what does the front of the trunk carry?
cards.a: 9% for the head and each arm; 18% for the front of the trunk.

cards.q: How is the first 8-hour half of the Parkland volume timed?
cards.a: Half the volume, counted from the time of burn, not arrival; fluid already given is deducted.

cards.q: What hourly urine output do you aim for in an adult and in a child?
cards.a: Adult 0.5 mL/kg/h (30 to 50 mL/h); child 1 mL/kg/h. High output means reduce the fluid rate.

cards.q: Which topical agent penetrates eschar, and what does it cause?
cards.a: Mafenide penetrates eschar and can cause metabolic acidosis; silver sulfadiazine causes leucopenia and silver nitrate causes hyponatraemia.
